common_name: Valley Forge Elm (Highly Disease-Tolerant American Elm)

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Valley Forge, released by the USDA National Arboretum, ranks among the very highest of all American elm cultivars for Dutch elm disease tolerance, though it grows with a somewhat looser, faster habit than Princeton and benefits from early structural pruning.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the tree room for its broad, classic vase-shaped canopy. Valley Forge was released by the USDA National Arboretum after extensive screening trials and stands out for having some of the strongest documented Dutch elm disease tolerance of any American elm cultivar, making it a leading choice for restoring the American elm to streets and parks where the species was once devastated by the disease. It grows quickly, often faster than other resistant cultivars, though its structure can be somewhat more open and irregular, so early formative pruning helps develop a strong central framework as the tree matures. Water deeply while establishing, avoid trunk and root wounds that can allow disease entry, and expect a large, long-lived shade tree well suited to the wide, open sites where American elm has always excelled.

common_name: New Harmony Elm (Disease-Tolerant Upright American Elm)

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; New Harmony, released alongside Valley Forge by the USDA National Arboretum, combines strong Dutch elm disease tolerance with a more upright, compact habit than some other resistant selections.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. New Harmony was released by the USDA National Arboretum as a companion selection to Valley Forge, chosen from the same disease-screening program for combining strong Dutch elm disease tolerance with a somewhat more upright, uniform growth habit that some growers prefer for street and boulevard plantings. Like other resistant American elm cultivars it restores the tall, graceful, arching form long associated with the species, and it has performed reliably in urban conditions including compacted soil, heat, and air pollution. Water deeply during the establishment years, prune early to encourage a strong central leader and well-spaced scaffold branches, and allow ample overhead and root space for the tree's eventual large size.

common_name: Accolade Elm (Vigorous Disease-Resistant Hybrid Shade Tree)
scientific_name: Ulmus davidiana var. japonica × Ulmus wilsoniana 'Morton'

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in a wide range of soils in full sun; Accolade, introduced by the Morton Arboretum, is an Asian-species hybrid rather than an American elm selection and carries excellent, broad resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where the tree quickly develops a dense, vase-to-rounded canopy of glossy, dark green foliage. Accolade is a hybrid of two Asian elm species introduced by the Morton Arboretum, prized for combining rapid growth, strong urban tolerance, and outstanding resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle, two of the biggest threats to elms in cultivation. Unlike American elm selections it does not aim to replicate the classic broad vase silhouette exactly, instead forming a somewhat more upright, uniform shade tree well suited to streets, parking areas, and residential landscapes where a fast-growing, trouble-free canopy tree is wanted. It tolerates heat, drought once established, and a range of soil types, and needs only routine formative pruning in its early years to develop strong branch structure.
